## The Rule

**Invoke relevant or requested skills BEFORE any response or action** — including clarifying questions, exploring the codebase, or checking files. If it turns out wrong for the situation, you don't have to use it.

**Before entering plan mode:** if you haven't already brainstormed, invoke the brainstorming skill first.

## Skill Priority

When multiple skills apply, process skills come first — they set the approach, then implementation skills (frontend-design, etc.) carry it out. Brainstorming and systematic-debugging are Superpowers' most common process skills, but the rule holds for any of them.

- "Let's build X" → superpowers:brainstorming first, then implementation skills.
- "Fix this bug" → superpowers:systematic-debugging first, then domain skills.

| "I need more context first" | Skill check comes BEFORE clarifying questions. |
| "Let me explore the codebase first" | Skills tell you HOW to explore. Check first. |
| "I can check git/files quickly" | Files lack conversation context. Check for skills. |
| "Let me gather information first" | Skills tell you HOW to gather information. |
| "This doesn't need a formal skill" | If a skill exists, use it. |
| "I remember this skill" | Skills evolve. Read current version. |

| "The skill is overkill" | Simple things become complex. Use it. |
| "I'll just do this one thing first" | Check BEFORE doing anything. |
| "This feels productive" | Undisciplined action wastes time. Skills prevent this. |

## claude.ai Supabase
Here are guidelines for using Supabase tools effectively:

- Before making schema changes, use `list_tables` to understand the existing structure
- When debugging issues, start with `get_logs` and `get_advisors` before making changes
- Use `get_project_url` and `get_publishable_api_key` when helping users configure client-side integrations

If you have access to a local development environment with a filesystem and shell:
- Install the Supabase agent skill for critical development and security guidance: `npx skills add supabase/agent-skills` (https://supabase.com/docs/guides/getting-started/ai-skills.md)
- Use the Supabase CLI (`supabase`) for local development workflows such as starting a local stack, managing migrations, and running edge functions locally (https://supabase.com/docs/guides/local-development.md)
- Prefer local development and testing before applying changes to a remote project

If you are running in a web-only or remote environment without filesystem or shell access:
- Rely on the MCP tools directly for all Supabase interactions
- Use `apply_migration` carefully, as changes go directly to the remote project

- design: Create a design canvas - a multi-artboard visual design published as an Artifact that runs Claude Design's canvas editor (an early preview of Claude Design inside Claude Code). You DRAFT the design as .dc.html artboards laid out on one pan/zoom canvas; where saving is enabled for the user's account they refine every element visually (click-to-select, a properties panel, inline text editing, undo/redo) and Save publishes a new version for everyone, otherwise they get a view-and-export (PNG/PDF) preview of your draft. Good for UI mockups and screen flows, landing pages, marketing and social graphics, and print pieces - posters, flyers, brochures as single-page artboards; memos and reports as one flowing artboard. Use when someone wants a design, mockup, wireframe, UI or screen design, landing page, poster, flyer, brochure, banner, card, one-pager, or any visual layout they would rather tweak by hand than in code. Only for CREATING or re-seeding a canvas; an existing one is edited in its published Artifact.
- dataviz: Use this skill whenever you are about to create ANY chart, graph, plot, dashboard, or data visualization, in ANY output medium — an HTML or React artifact, inline SVG, plotting code in any library (matplotlib, plotly, d3, Recharts, …), an image/PNG you will render and upload, or a chart shared into Slack. Read it BEFORE writing the first line of chart code, choosing chart colors, building a stat tile / meter / KPI row, or laying out a dashboard. Produces visualizations that read as one system — elegant, accessible, consistent in light and dark — using a brand-neutral placeholder palette you swap for your own. Teaches a design-system-agnostic method: a form heuristic, a color formula with a runnable validator, mark specs, and interaction rules. A validated default palette is documented in `references/palette.md` — swap that file's values for your brand's. Triggers on: "chart", "graph", "plot", "data viz", "visualization", "dashboard", "analytics", "visualize data", "categorical colors", "sequential / diverging palette", "stat tile", "sparkline", "heatmap", "legend", "axis", "tooltip", "chart colors", "color by series".
- artifact-design: Design guidance and fundamentals for Artifacts. - Load before writing any artifact, including a skill-instructed Markdown one - Markdown is never a shortcut past the design pass.
- artifact-diagramming: Diagramming know-how for Artifacts - when a picture earns its place, how to draw one that shows the real mechanism, and the inline-SVG mechanics that keep it legible in both themes.
- artifact-capabilities: Runtime capabilities a published Artifact page can be granted — behavior static HTML cannot provide on its own, such as the page reading live or connected data, remembering what people do on it (a poll, a sign-up sheet, a checklist, a document edited in place — it saves new versions of itself), keeping state shared across viewers, knowing who is viewing, asking Claude a question of its own, storing files people add, or handing the viewer a file to save. Serves this user's live capability roster and the typed call definitions. Load it whenever the user asks for an artifact needing any such runtime behavior.
- update-config: Use this skill to configure the Claude Code harness via settings.json. Automated behaviors ("from now on when X", "each time X", "whenever X", "before/after X") require hooks configured in settings.json - the harness executes these, not Claude, so memory/preferences cannot fulfill them. Also use for: permissions ("allow X", "add permission", "move permission to"), env vars ("set X=Y"), hook troubleshooting, or any changes to settings.json/settings.local.json files. Examples: "allow npm commands", "add bq permission to global settings", "move permission to user settings", "set DEBUG=true", "when claude stops show X". For simple settings like theme/model, suggest the /config command.
- keybindings-help: Use when the user wants to customize keyboard shortcuts, rebind keys, add chord bindings, or modify ~/.claude/keybindings.json. Examples: "rebind ctrl+s", "add a chord shortcut", "change the submit key", "customize keybindings".
- code-review: Review the current diff, or a PR number/branch/path target, for correctness bugs and reuse/simplification/efficiency cleanups at the given effort level (low/medium: fewer, high-confidence findings; high→max: broader coverage, may include uncertain findings; ultra: deep multi-agent review in the cloud); with no level given, it reuses the level you typed last. Pass --comment to post findings as inline PR comments, or --fix to apply the findings to the working tree after the review. For ultra on a GitHub.com PR target, --post asks to post the finished review’s findings to the PR as a single comment from the user’s GitHub account (not a review; the launch dialog still confirms in interactive sessions, while non-interactive mode posts on the flag alone) and --no-post hides that option.
- simplify: Review the changed code for reuse, simplification, efficiency, and altitude cleanups, then apply the fixes. Quality only — it does not hunt for bugs; use /code-review for that.
- fewer-permission-prompts: Scan your transcripts for common read-only Bash and MCP tool calls, then add a prioritized allowlist to project .claude/settings.json to reduce permission prompts.
- loop: Run a prompt or slash command on a recurring interval (e.g. /loop 5m /foo). Omit the interval to let the model self-pace. - When the user wants to set up a recurring task, poll for status, or run something repeatedly on an interval (e.g. "check the deploy every 5 minutes", "keep running /babysit-prs"). Do NOT invoke for one-off tasks.
- schedule: Create, update, list, or run scheduled cloud agents (routines) that execute on a cron schedule. - When the user wants to schedule a recurring cloud agent, set up automated tasks, create a cron job for Claude Code, or manage their scheduled agents/routines. Also use when the user wants a one-time scheduled run ("run this once at 3pm", "remind me to check X tomorrow").
- claude-api: Reference for the Claude API / Anthropic SDK — model ids, pricing, params, streaming, tool use, MCP, agents, caching, token counting, model migration.
TRIGGER — read BEFORE opening the target file; don't skip because it "looks like a one-liner" — whenever: the prompt names Claude/Anthropic in any form (Claude, Anthropic, Fable, Opus, Sonnet, Haiku, `anthropic`, `@anthropic-ai`, `claude-*`, `us.anthropic.*`, `[1m]`); the user asks about an LLM (pricing/model choice/limits/caching) — never answer from memory; OR the task is LLM-shaped with provider unstated (agent/MCP/tool-definition/multi-agent/RAG/LLM-judge/computer-use; generate/summarize/extract/classify/rewrite/converse over NL; debugging refusals/cutoffs/streaming/tool-calls/tokens).

Opens pages in new tabs within your existing Chrome session. # Session Handoff / Project State

Command:resume

_Last updated: 2026-08-27 (**`main` = `1fa8790`. PRs #46–#52 MERGED. #53 OPEN and green** —
`feat/packing-trip-list`. **Packing mode is BUILT end to end**: plan → capsule → days → shortfall,
pin/remove/swap, persisted, Pro-gated, recorded. **Two licence decisions this session: OpenWeather
replaces Open-Meteo (clean, ODbL); the cutout AGPL/DIS5K question is still open.** Next:
`todo/2026-08-27-openweather-swap.md`.) Read this first when resuming._

## Where things actually are — 2026-08-27

### Merged this session
| PR | what |
|---|---|
| #46 | Image weight — closet grid −80%, diary −80%, item detail −64% |
| #47 | Capture: contrast guidance + Retake (which also closed the abandoned-upload leak at source) |
| #48 | The capsule engine — pure logic, calibrated on the real closet |
| #50 | Packing end to end + day variety (**#49 was closed as redundant — #50 was stacked on it and carried its commits**) |
| #51 | Sentry build fix + packing navigation |
| #52 | Over-packing fix + the piece sheet |

**#53 is open and green** — the trips list.

### ⚠️ Still open, in priority order

1. **`todo/2026-08-27-openweather-swap.md`** — the launch blocker. Plan written, not started.
2. **`beyondHorizon` is computed and thrown away** (`app/packing/[tripId]/page.tsx` hard-codes
   `false`). ⚠️ **The swap makes this worse: One Call gives 8 days where Open-Meteo gave 16**, so
   every trip 9–16 days out newly falls past the horizon. It is Task 6 of that plan.
3. **`editCapsule` re-narrates on EVERY edit** — one Haiku call per pin/remove/swap. Recorded in
   `generation_events` as `kind='trip'`, but nothing meters it. Cheapest fix: only re-narrate days
   whose pieces changed, or debounce.
4. **The cutout licence** — `todo/2026-08-26-own-the-cutout-pipeline.md`, and the DIS5K email sent
   2026-08-25 with no reply expected.
5. #14 route-url-audit · #16 design audit · e2e Task 3 (deferred into #16).

---

## ⚠️ TWO LICENCE PROBLEMS — one solved, one not

### ✅ Weather — SOLVED 2026-08-27. OpenWeather One Call 4.0

Open-Meteo's free API is not licensed for commercial use and is on the critical path of every
generate. **Replaced by OpenWeather One Call 4.0**, self-service.

- **ODbL. Commercial use allowed.** Verbatim: does **NOT** require you to open-source your
  application, share your product code, or disclose your business logic. **No business licence
  needed.**
- 1,000 calls/day free, then per-call. **Cache per rounded location per day in POSTGRES**, so calls
  scale with cities rather than users. (`roundCoord`, 2dp ≈ 1.1km, already exists for exactly this.)
- ⚠️ **Obligation 1: visible attribution** — `Weather data © OpenWeather`, on the screen where the
  weather appears. A help-centre article is "too obscure"; a settings sub-page is "not visible".
  **Placement deferred by the user; the requirement is not.**
- ⚠️ **Obligation 2: the cache must never become a public endpoint.** ODbL ShareAlike attaches to a
  weather dataset or API made available *outside the organisation*. Internal caching is fine.

⚠️ **CORRECTION worth keeping:** an earlier note here claimed self-service was CC BY-SA with
ShareAlike over the *application*, and that a paid business licence was needed to escape copyleft.
**That was wrong** — it came from a search summary about One Call 3.0. The user produced
OpenWeather's own explainer. Primary source beat summary, as it should.

### ⚠️ Cutouts — STILL OPEN

`@imgly/background-removal` is **AGPL-3.0**, dual-licensed, running in every user's browser. And the
ISNet weights it ships were trained on **DIS5K**, whose Terms are non-commercial by default.
⚠️ **BiRefNet and BEN2 are DIS5K-trained too** — free of charge is not free of the clause.

- **Email sent 2026-08-25** to Xuebin Qin for DIS5K commercial permission. Expect silence; two weeks,
  one follow-up, then treat as unresolved. Draft: `docs/dis5k-permission-request.md`.
- **Track A step 2** — own the pipeline on `onnxruntime-web` — is NOT blocked on that reply.
  Different problem, different owner.
- ⚠️ **"Free options only" (2026-08-25) was scoped to the CUTOUT question, not a policy.** The user
  chose a paid weather API on 2026-08-27, so paying is demonstrably on the table. **IMG.LY's
  commercial licence is the one quote nobody has asked for.**

---

## ⚠️ Lessons this session cost something to learn

Kept because git cannot tell you any of them.

1. **Textbook greedy set-cover cannot solve a capsule.** An outfit is CONJUNCTIVE (top AND bottom AND
   shoes), so no single item covers any day until all three are present — every candidate gains zero,
   the loop exits, the capsule is empty. The solve walks days in order instead, dressing each from
   what is already packed before falling back.

=== openweather-swap ===
# OpenWeather Swap Implementation Plan

> **For agentic workers:** REQUIRED SUB-SKILL: Use superpowers:subagent-driven-development (recommended) or superpowers:executing-plans to implement this plan task-by-task. Steps use checkbox (`- [ ]`) syntax for tracking.

**Goal:** Replace Open-Meteo with OpenWeather One Call 4.0, cached per location per day in Postgres,
so the generator runs on a provider that is licensed for commercial use.

**Architecture:** One adapter swap behind the existing `Weather` type, plus a read-through Postgres
cache so calls scale with distinct cities per day rather than with users. Nothing above
`lib/weather/` changes shape.

**Tech Stack:** TypeScript 6, Supabase Postgres, Vitest, Playwright.

**Spec:** [`../scoping/2026-08-27-weather-provider-swap.md`](../scoping/2026-08-27-weather-provider-swap.md)

## Global Constraints

- ⚠️ **This is a LAUNCH BLOCKER, not an optimisation.** Open-Meteo's free API is not permitted for
  commercial use and every drop, reroll, styled look and trip reads it.
- ⚠️ **`Weather` (`lib/generator/rules.ts`) must not change shape.** Everything downstream — scoring,
  `weatherRules`, `planningTempFor`, `laterAdvice` — is tested against it. A provider swap that
  changes the domain type is a rewrite, not a swap.
- ⚠️ **Attribution is REQUIRED to ship:** `Weather data © OpenWeather`, visible, on the screen where
  weather appears. Their explainer marks a help-centre article "too obscure" and a settings sub-page
  "not visible".
- ⚠️ **The cache must NEVER be exposed as an endpoint.** ODbL ShareAlike attaches to a weather
  dataset or API made available outside the organisation. Internal caching is fine; a public route
  over it is not.
- ⚠️ **The horizon SHRINKS: 16 days → 8.** Trips 9–16 days out move from real forecast to stand-in.
- Secrets server-side only. `OPENWEATHER_API_KEY` in `.env.local`, never `NEXT_PUBLIC_`.
- Lint baseline is 13 problems; "clean" means unchanged, not zero.

---

### Task 1: The cache table

**Files:** Create `supabase/migrations/2026XXXXXXXXXX_weather_cache.sql`

⚠️ **Why a table and not `revalidate`:** Next's Data Cache is per-deployment, not guaranteed shared
across instances or regions, and gone on redeploy. Decision 6 records the sibling trap — `use cache`
is in-memory and dies with the instance. A table is free, durable and shared by every user in a city.
This is also where the Redis question already landed: rejected, because Postgres already is the cache.

- [ ] **Step 1:** Write the migration.

```sql
-- Weather is identical for everyone in a place on a day, so it is cached per
-- place per day rather than per user. `roundCoord` (2dp ≈ 1.1km) already
-- normalises the key at the boundary — that is why it exists.
create table if not exists public.weather_cache (
  lat        numeric(6,2) not null,
  lon        numeric(6,2) not null,
  day        date         not null,
  -- The MAPPED payload, never the provider's raw response: a future swap should
  -- touch one adapter, not every reader.
  payload    jsonb        not null,
  fetched_at timestamptz  not null default now(),
  primary key (lat, lon, day)
);

alter table public.weather_cache enable row level security;

-- Readable by any signed-in user; written only by the server (service role, or
-- a server action running as the user — see Task 3 Step 4). It holds no user
-- data, but a table with no policy is either wide open or unreachable.
create policy "weather_cache_read" on public.weather_cache
  for select using (auth.uid() is not null);

grant select on public.weather_cache to authenticated;
```

- [ ] **Step 2:** Apply and confirm RLS is on and the primary key is the composite.
- [ ] **Step 3: Commit.**

---

### Task 2: The adapter

**Files:** Create `lib/weather/openweather.ts`, `lib/weather/__tests__/openweather.test.ts`

**Interfaces:**
```ts
export function mapOneCall(raw: OneCallResponse, nowIso?: string): MappedForecast;
export function mapOneCallDaily(raw: OneCallResponse, dates: string[]): TripForecast;
export const OWM_RAIN_IDS: Set<number>;
```

⚠️ **Pure mapping only — no `fetch` in this file.** That is what makes it testable against captured
fixtures, and it is how `open-meteo.ts` is already split.

- [ ] **Step 1: Capture a real response as a fixture.** One `curl` against One Call 4.0 for a known
  city, saved to `lib/weather/__tests__/fixtures/onecall.json`. ⚠️ **Strip the API key** before
  committing, and check the file for coordinates that identify anyone.

- [ ] **Step 2: Write the failing test.** Assert against the fixture that:
  - `tempC` / `highC` / `lowC` come from the DAILY block, and the look is built for the HIGH
    (`rules.ts` documents why: a look worn all day must not be chosen for the minute the app opened)
  - `rain` is true for OpenWeather's rain condition ids and false for clear
  - hourly cells still feed `planningTempFor` — ⚠️ **One Call gives 48 hourly, Open-Meteo gave 24**
  - a response missing `daily` degrades rather than throwing

- [ ] **Step 3: Implement.** ⚠️ **`RAIN_CODES` does not transfer.** Open-Meteo uses WMO codes;
  OpenWeather uses its own condition ids (2xx thunderstorm, 3xx drizzle, 5xx rain, 6xx snow). Map
  them explicitly and test both a rain id and a clear one — a silently-empty rain set means the rain
  guard never fires and nobody notices until it rains.

- [ ] **Step 4:** Run and confirm pass. **Commit.**

---

### Task 3: The read-through cache

**Files:** Create `lib/weather/cache.ts`, `lib/weather/__tests__/cache.test.ts`

**Interfaces:**
```ts
export async function cachedForecast(lat: number, lon: number, day: string,
  fetcher: () => Promise<unknown>): Promise<MappedForecast>;
```

- [ ] **Step 1: Write the failing test** with an injected fetcher and a fake store:
  - a miss calls the fetcher once and stores the mapped payload
  - a hit does NOT call the fetcher
  - ⚠️ **two concurrent misses for the same key call the fetcher once, or the insert conflict is
    swallowed** — a city waking up at 8am is exactly the concurrent case, and a crash there is a
    blank weather strip for everyone in it
  - ⚠️ **a fetcher failure returns the STALE row if one exists** rather than throwing. A day-old
    temperature is a far better outcome than a screen with no weather.

- [ ] **Step 2: Implement**, `on conflict do nothing` on the insert.

- [ ] **Step 3:** ⚠️ **Cache the DAILY block only.** The codebase already draws this line:
  *"`daily` is what the LOOK is built for; `current` is what the screen shows."* Caching `current`
  for a whole day means the weather pill reads the 8am temperature at 6pm. Either keep a short
  `revalidate` for the current reading or accept the staleness **explicitly, in a comment**.

- [ ] **Step 4:** ⚠️ Decide and record how the row is WRITTEN. The read is `authenticated`; the write
  needs either a service-role path or an insert policy. **Do not widen the read policy to cover
  writes** — a table any user can write is a table any user can poison.

# Cutout Backfill Implementation Plan

> **For agentic workers:** REQUIRED SUB-SKILL: Use superpowers:subagent-driven-development (recommended) or superpowers:executing-plans to implement this plan task-by-task. Steps use checkbox (`- [ ]`) syntax for tracking.

**Goal:** Re-encode the PNG cutouts already in Storage as WebP, so existing closets get the same ~75% size drop new uploads get.

**Architecture:** The WebP plan only affects new captures — every garment uploaded before it keeps its 540–714 KB PNG forever. A one-off Node script walks `items` rows whose `cutout_url` ends in `.png`, re-encodes with `sharp` (preserving alpha), uploads the WebP alongside, and updates the row. It is idempotent, resumable, and dry-run by default. The old PNG is left in place until the run is verified.

**Tech Stack:** `sharp` (dev-only), `@supabase/supabase-js` with the service role, `tsx`.

## Global Constraints

- **Requires `docs/superpowers/plans/done/2026-07-22-webp-cutouts.md`** — merged, so new uploads are already WebP. (Backfilling before that shipped would have meant running it twice.)
- `sharp` is a **devDependency and a script-only import**. It must never be imported from `app/` or `lib/` — client-side, zero-cost image work is Decision 2, and this script is maintenance tooling, not app code.
- The service-role key is used **only here**, in a script run by hand, never in app code (which relies exclusively on RLS). Read it from the environment; never commit it.
- **Non-destructive.** Write the `.webp`, update the row, leave the `.png`. Deleting originals is a separate, later decision once the run is proven.
- Idempotent: re-running must skip rows already migrated, so an interrupted run can simply be run again.

# Route & URL Audit Implementation Plan

> **For agentic workers:** REQUIRED SUB-SKILL: Use superpowers:subagent-driven-development (recommended) or superpowers:executing-plans to implement this plan task-by-task. Steps use checkbox (`- [ ]`) syntax for tracking.

**Goal:** Bring routing, URLs, navigation and cache invalidation in line with the app the daily-drop model turned Fitcheck into.

**Architecture:** The current routing was designed for a live generator: `/generate` is a verb, occasion lives only in React state, no look has a URL, and nothing revalidates when outfits are written. - **Run last.** Requires the daily-looks plan; reads best after intent-first, since that decides what the entry screen shows.
- Renaming a route is user-visible: old URLs must redirect, not 404. The app is an installed PWA — a stale `start_url` opens a dead page on someone's home screen.
- No new API route handlers in this plan. Those belong to Phase 2 (share cards, push, cron).
- Do not build the Diary feature here. `wear_logs` stays unused; this plan only stops `/calendar` being unreachable nonsense.
- TDD where there is logic; routing changes are verified in the iOS Simulator.

# End-to-end tests — the Playwright foundation

> **For agentic workers:** REQUIRED SUB-SKILL: Use superpowers:executing-plans to implement this plan
> task-by-task. Steps use checkbox (`- [ ]`) syntax for tracking.

**Goal:** Cover the journeys a user actually walks, in a real browser, against a real database — so the
class of defect that has repeatedly escaped this project's unit tests gets caught by CI instead of by
the user.

**Architecture:** Playwright against `next start` and the local Supabase stack, with a **seeded,
deterministic test user** whose data the tests own. Unit tests keep doing what they are good at; this
adds the layer above them.

**Tech Stack:** Playwright, Next.js 16.3.1, Supabase (local), TypeScript 6.

## Why this plan exists, stated honestly

**User decision, 2026-08-19: *"i want playwright with e2e tests, unit tests are not so good."*** The
record backs that up. Sorting every defect found in the 2026-08-13 → 08-19 stretch by what caught it:

| Caught by a unit test | Caught only by real data on a real screen |
|---|---|
| The plan's own contradictory warmth test (#32) | *"Unlocks 258 new outfits"* — true and uncredible |
| `Denim`/`Canvas` at 0.5 being indistinguishable from unscored | A camel overcoat could never be recommended |
| A linen shirt lifted by the winter floor | The reason line contradicting the recommendation |
| The first coat scoring zero | *"You have 1 coats against 10 tops"* |
| | *"Adds 1% more outfits"* for a closet that can build none |
| | *"Up to 3° this afternoon — you're dressed for it"* at −2°C |
| | The re-ranker told the wrong temperature |

# Own the cutout pipeline — drop the AGPL wrapper

> **For agentic workers:** REQUIRED SUB-SKILL: Use superpowers:executing-plans to implement this plan
> task-by-task. Steps use checkbox (`- [ ]`) syntax for tracking.

**Goal:** Run the same segmentation we run today, on our own `onnxruntime-web` (MIT) pipeline, and
delete `@imgly/background-removal` (AGPL-3.0) from the bundle. **No quality regression** — that is the
acceptance criterion, not a hope.

**Architecture:** Replace one library call with four steps we own — decode → preprocess → ONNX session
→ postprocess. Same ISNet model, same input size, same output shape. Everything stays client-side; the
zero-marginal-cost bargain of Decision 2 is unchanged.

**Tech Stack:** TypeScript 6, `onnxruntime-web` (MIT), WebAssembly / optional WebGPU, Canvas, Vitest,
Playwright/WebKit.

---

## Why this exists, and what it does NOT fix

`@imgly/background-removal` is **AGPL-3.0** and dual-licensed (*"contact support@img.ly for questions
about other licensing options"*). It is downloaded and executed in every user's browser, which the
**FSF's own guidance** treats as *conveying* — legally like shipping a binary, not like SaaS. The FSF
licence FAQ further holds that JavaScript combined into a single program with AGPL code puts the whole
combined work under copyleft absent an explicit exception, and IMG.LY grants none. *Artifex v. Hancom*
established that these licences are enforceable as contract **and** copyright, and Artifex runs the
identical dual-licence business model.

Full analysis: `scoping/2026-08-25-cutout-quality-scoping.md` §1, §9b.

# Own the cutout pipeline — drop the AGPL wrapper

> **For agentic workers:** REQUIRED SUB-SKILL: Use superpowers:executing-plans to implement this plan
> task-by-task. Steps use checkbox (`- [ ]`) syntax for tracking.

**Goal:** Run the same segmentation we run today, on our own `onnxruntime-web` (MIT) pipeline, and
delete `@imgly/background-removal` (AGPL-3.0) from the bundle. **No quality regression** — that is the
acceptance criterion, not a hope.

**Architecture:** Replace one library call with four steps we own — decode → preprocess → ONNX session
→ postprocess. Same ISNet model, same input size, same output shape. Everything stays client-side; the
zero-marginal-cost bargain of Decision 2 is unchanged.

**Tech Stack:** TypeScript 6, `onnxruntime-web` (MIT), WebAssembly / optional WebGPU, Canvas, Vitest,
Playwright/WebKit.

---

## Why this exists, and what it does NOT fix

`@imgly/background-removal` is **AGPL-3.0** and dual-licensed (*"contact support@img.ly for questions
about other licensing options"*). It is downloaded and executed in every user's browser, which the
**FSF's own guidance** treats as *conveying* — legally like shipping a binary, not like SaaS. The FSF
licence FAQ further holds that JavaScript combined into a single program with AGPL code puts the whole
combined work under copyleft absent an explicit exception, and IMG.LY grants none. *Artifex v. Hancom*
established that these licences are enforceable as contract **and** copyright, and Artifex runs the
identical dual-licence business model.

I read `docs/STATE.md`, every plan in `docs/superpowers/plans/{todo,scoping}`, and checked git/GitHub directly.

## First: STATE.md was stale, now fixed

It said "#53 OPEN and green, `main` = `1fa8790`". Git says **#53 merged as `015c554`** — packing mode is fully landed, nothing is in flight. I corrected the TL;DR. You're sitting on `feat/packing-trip-list`, which is merged; next work starts from `main`.

## Where you are

Packing mode is done end to end (PRs #46–#53): plan → capsule → days → shortfall, pin/remove/swap, persisted, Pro-gated, recorded, and now listable. That was the whole arc of the last two sessions.

## The queue, in the order STATE ranks it

**1. OpenWeather swap — `todo/2026-08-27-openweather-swap.md`. The launch blocker.**
Open-Meteo's free tier isn't licensed for commercial use and sits on the critical path of *every* generate. Plan is written, 7 tasks, not started:

| Task | What |
|---|---|
| 1 | `weather_cache` table — Postgres, keyed `(lat, lon, day)`, not `revalidate` (per-deployment, dies on redeploy) |
| 2 | `lib/weather/openweather.ts` — pure mapper, fixture-tested. ⚠️ `RAIN_CODES` doesn't transfer: WMO → OWM condition ids |
| 3 | Read-through cache — concurrent-miss safety, stale-row fallback, cache the **daily** block not `current` |
| 4 | Swap callers, `FORECAST_DAYS_MAX` 16 → **8** |
| 5 | Attribution — `Weather data © OpenWeather`, visible, on the weather strip and day cards |
| 6 | `beyondHorizon` wired for real |
| 7 | Verify — incl. proving the cache saves calls and the tests actually go red |

Three decisions in that plan are still yours, not the implementer's: **where the attribution sits** (you deferred placement, the requirement stands), **whether the current-temp pill gets its own short cache** or accepts day-stale, and whether climate normals become a follow-up plan.

**2. `beyondHorizon` is computed and thrown away.** `mapTripForecast` sets it correctly; `app/packing/[tripId]/page.tsx` hard-codes `false`. A trip past the window renders a capsule built on the nearest real day's weather, **presented as fact**. It's Task 6 above and it stops being an edge case the moment the horizon shrinks to 8 days — every trip 9–16 days out newly falls past it.

**3. `editCapsule` re-narrates on every edit.** One Haiku call per pin/remove/swap. Recorded as `kind='trip'` in `generation_events`, but unmetered. Cheapest fix: re-narrate only changed days, or debounce. Small enough that it doesn't need its own plan.

**4. The cutout licence — still open.** `@imgly/background-removal` is AGPL-3.0 running in every browser, and its ISNet weights are DIS5K-trained (non-commercial by default). Email sent 2026-08-25, no reply expected — two weeks then treat as unresolved. `todo/2026-08-26-own-the-cutout-pipeline.md` (move to `onnxruntime-web`) is **not** blocked on that reply. STATE flags one thing nobody has done: **ask IMG.LY for a commercial quote.** "Free options only" was scoped to the cutout question; you paid for weather on the 27th, so paying is demonstrably on the table.

**5. Then, in order:** `route-url-audit` (#14, designed to run last — `/generate` → `/today`, occasion in the URL, manifest `start_url`), then the **full design audit** (#16, `impeccable` + `design-taste-frontend` at phone width), which also absorbs e2e Task 3.

**Parked deliberately:** notifications (deferred — gate is installs, not a native app), cutout-backfill (conditional, nothing to convert), wear-stats (#10, blocked on a design decision), women's wardrobe and stylist-chat (scoping only, need a brainstorm before a plan).

## My recommendation

Start the OpenWeather swap, but answer the attribution-placement question first — it's Task 5 and it's a design call you already deferred once. Fold Task 6 in as written rather than splitting it; the horizon shrink makes the honest flag part of the swap, not a follow-up.

Want me to open a branch and begin, or brainstorm the attribution placement first?

content.text:
Good question — it's the one thing in the plan that's a design call rather than an implementation detail. Here's the actual constraint.

## What the licence requires

OpenWeather's self-service tier is ODbL. Commercial use is fine, no business licence needed, but there's one obligation: **visible credit — `Weather data © OpenWeather` — on the screen where the weather appears.** Their own explainer explicitly rejects the two easy hiding places: a help-centre article is *"too obscure"* and a settings sub-page is *"not visible"*. So we can't tuck it into Settings → About and call it done.

## Why it's a design problem, not a footer

Two screens show weather:

- **The Stylist's weather strip** (`components/generate/weather-strip.tsx:41`) — temp, condition, city, feels-like, plus a collapsible hourly row
- **The packing day cards** (`components/packing/day-list.tsx:80`) — a temp in each card's header corner

The trap: the instinctive move is to set the credit tiny and faint so it vanishes. But `DESIGN.md:130` sets the **readability floor at Warm Gray `#928C7F`** — Dim (`#615C52`) and Faint (`#52504A`) are ornament only and fail contrast. So setting it in Faint would break the design system *and* arguably fail OpenWeather's "visible" test at the same time. It has to be real text, at the floor colour. That's why the plan says screenshot it in the simulator and judge it rather than just adding a line.

So the decision is **which surface carries it, and whether it's always on screen or behind a tap.**

# Weather provider swap — Open-Meteo → OpenWeather

_Decided 2026-08-27. Not a TDD plan yet — the shape is settled, the sequencing is not._

## Why

**Open-Meteo's free API is not permitted for commercial use**, and after the weather work of
2026-08-13 → 15 it is the backbone of the generator: every drop, every reroll, every styled look and
now every trip reads it. `docs/STATE.md` has called it *"the only item that can stop a launch"* since
2026-08-12. This is the fix.

## The decision

**OpenWeather One Call API 4.0**, self-service. <https://openweathermap.org/api/one-call-4>

| | |
|---|---|
| Free allowance | **1,000 calls/day**, then per-call |
| Licence | **ODbL — commercial use allowed** |
| Requires open-sourcing? | **No.** Verbatim: does *not* require you to open-source your application, share your product code, or disclose your business logic |
| Obligation | **Visible attribution**: `Weather data © OpenWeather` |

⚠️ **CORRECTION worth keeping.** An earlier reading of this (from a search summary about One Call
3.0) said self-service carried CC BY-SA ShareAlike over the *application*, and that a paid business
licence would be needed to escape copyleft. **That was wrong.** OpenWeather's own licence explainer
is unambiguous: self-service is ODbL and the app is unaffected. No business licence is needed. The
primary source beat the summary, as it should.

## ⚠️ Share-Alike exists, and it constrains the cache — not the app

It attaches only if you build a reusable dataset, restructure/combine/enrich it, or operate your own
weather dataset or API from stored OpenWeather data — **and make that available outside your
organisation.**

Our cache IS stored OpenWeather data. What keeps it clear is that final clause: it serves our own
app and is never exposed.

> **Constraint, recorded now rather than rediscovered: the weather cache must never become a public
> endpoint.** The moment Fitcheck offers a weather API, however small, ODbL ShareAlike attaches to it.

## The cache — in Postgres, not in memory

**Calls should scale with distinct CITIES per day, not with users.** One person opening the app in
Zürich should pay for the whole city's forecast that day.

The codebase is already shaped for this: `roundCoord` (2dp ≈ 1.1 km) exists precisely so every caller
in one place produces the same key, and its comment says why — raw GPS precision would make every
user's URL unique and defeat the cache.

⚠️ **What is NOT sufficient:** `fetch(…, { next: { revalidate } })` alone. That is Next's Data Cache

content.text:
I've read the plan, the scoping doc, and the current `open-meteo.ts` / `trip.ts`. Three concerns, one of which I think is a real architectural correction. I'd rather raise them now than build twice.

## 1. ⚠️ The cache can't store `mapForecast`'s output — every field in it is now-relative

This is the big one. The plan says *"store the MAPPED payload, not the raw response"*. But look at what `mapForecast` actually returns (`lib/weather/open-meteo.ts:104`):

```
tempC, feelsLikeC, condition  → the CURRENT reading
hourly                        → 4 cells starting at now, isNow flag
restOfDay                     → hours remaining TODAY
highC / lowC                  → Math.max(...ahead) — the peak STILL AHEAD, not the day's
```

`highC`/`lowC` are deliberately *"the peak and trough STILL AHEAD, not the calendar day's"* — the comment says why: caching the calendar-day max would plan a 20:00 look against a 17:00 peak that's been and gone, the mirror of the sweater-on-a-34.8°-day bug.

So **literally every field except `timezone` depends on when you ask.** Cache that payload at 8am and read it at 6pm and you don't just get a stale pill — you get a look planned against a peak that already passed. That's the bug the code was specifically written to prevent.

**The fix:** cache the **time-invariant source** — the day's hourly cells + the daily high/low block — and run `mapForecast` per request against it. Still one API call per city per day; the economics are unchanged. It honours the plan's actual intent (no OpenWeather shape leaking into the cache) because we store *our* shape, just not collapsed to a now-relative view.

This makes the payload a time series rather than a `Weather`, which is a change to Task 3's stated interface.

## 2. One Call returns 8 days per response, but the cache key is per-day

`cachedForecast(lat, lon, day, fetcher)` is single-day. A trip needs 8. If a miss on day 5 triggers a fetch, that response *already contains* days 1–8 — so either one fetch writes all 8 rows, or a single trip costs 8 calls instead of 1.

That's the whole 1,000/day budget, and Task 7 Step 2 wouldn't catch it — it only tests two users, one city, one day.

**Recommendation:** one fetch fills every day it covers (`on conflict do nothing`), and the Stylist reads a single row from the same table. One table, one key, one call.

## 3. The write path contradicts a CLAUDE.md hard rule, and the plan leaves it open

Task 3 Step 4 says decide it; CLAUDE.md says *"there is no service-role bypass in app code."* The trap is that Supabase's PostgREST **is** a public endpoint — an `insert ... with check (true)` policy means any user with their own JWT can POST arbitrary rows and poison the forecast for everyone in their city. That's the plan's own *"a table any user can write is a table any user can poison"*, and it's the default outcome, not an edge case.

Yes — with one nuance worth being precise about, because it changes what "right" means.

**What you get:** we fetch **once** per city per day and store all 48 hourly cells. At read time we pick the cell for *your* hour. So someone opening the app at 8am and someone at 6pm both see their own hour's temperature, and the look is planned against the peak still ahead of them — from a **single** API call, not one per hour.

**The nuance:** we're not re-fetching hourly, so the 6pm reading is a *forecast made that morning*. Accurate as a forecast, but not refreshed. Since `fetched_at` is already in the table for exactly this, I'll add a staleness constant — **refresh if the row is older than 6 hours** — which costs at most 4 calls per city per day instead of 1. At the free tier that's still ~250 cities/day, and a 6-hour-old prediction of "this afternoon" is meaningfully better than an 18-hour-old one. Say the word if you'd rather I pin it at one call per day.

**service role, scoped to `lib/weather/cache.ts` alone.** This knowingly departs from CLAUDE.md's

`SECURITY DEFINER` function is exposed as RPC by PostgREST anyway, so it inherits the same problem
with more machinery. ⚠️ **`SUPABASE_SERVICE_ROLE_KEY` must never be imported outside that one file.**"""

old_i = """**Interfaces:**
```ts

  fetcher: () => Promise<unknown>): Promise<MappedForecast>;
```"""
new_i = """**Interfaces:**
```ts

  timezone: string;
  hourly: { time: string; tempC: number; feelsLikeC: number; conditionId: number }[];

The plan said *"store the MAPPED payload"*. Taken literally that is a **bug**, because every field
`mapForecast` returns is relative to the moment of asking:

| field | why it cannot be cached for a day |
|---|---|
| `tempC` / `feelsLikeC` / `condition` | the CURRENT reading |
| `hourly` | 4 cells starting at now, with an `isNow` flag |
| `restOfDay` | the hours remaining TODAY |
| `highC` / `lowC` | ⚠️ **the peak still AHEAD**, not the calendar day's |

That last row is the trap. `open-meteo.ts` computes high/low from `restOfDay` **on purpose** — its

and gone — the mirror of the bug that put a sweater on a 34.8°C day."* Caching a collapsed payload
reintroduces exactly that bug.

trip-shaped assertion: an 8-day trip must cause exactly ONE fetch.**

Base directory for this skill: /Users/1curafu/.claude/plugins/cache/claude-plugins-official/supabase/0.1.15/skills/supabase

# Supabase

## Core Principles

**1. Supabase changes frequently — verify against changelog and current docs before implementing.**
Do not rely on training data for Supabase features. Function signatures, config.toml settings, and API conventions change between versions.

First, fetch `https://supabase.com/changelog.md` (a lightweight summary index — not a heavy pull), scan for `breaking-change` tags relevant to your task, and follow the linked page for any that apply. Then look up the relevant topic using the documentation access methods below.

**2. Verify your work.**
After implementing any fix, run a test query to confirm the change works. A fix without verification is incomplete.

**3. Recover from errors, don't loop.**
If an approach fails after 2-3 attempts, stop and reconsider. Try a different method, check documentation, inspect the error more carefully, and review relevant logs when available. Supabase issues are not always solved by retrying the same command, and the answer is not always in the logs, but logs are often worth checking before proceeding.

**4. Exposing tables to the Data API:** Depending on the user's [Data API settings](https://supabase.com/dashboard/project/<ref>/integrations/data_api/settings), newly created tables may not be automatically exposed via the Data (REST) API. If this is the case, `anon` and `authenticated` roles will need to be explicitly granted access.

> Note that this is separate from RLS, which controls which _rows_ are visible once a table is accessible, not whether the table is accessible at all.

When a user reports a SQL-created table is unexpectedly inaccessible, check their Data API settings and whether the roles have been granted access via explicit `GRANT` SQL. When granting public (`anon`/`authenticated`) access, always enable RLS too. See [Exposing a Table to the Data API](https://supabase.com/docs/guides/api/securing-your-api.md) for the full setup workflow.

**5. RLS in exposed schemas.**
Enable RLS on every table in any exposed schema, which includes `public` by default. This is critical in Supabase because tables in exposed schemas can be reachable through the Data API when the `anon`/`authenticated` roles have access (see [Exposing a Table to the Data API](https://supabase.com/docs/guides/api/securing-your-api.md)). For private schemas, prefer RLS as defense in depth. After enabling RLS, create policies that match the actual access model rather than defaulting every table to the same `auth.uid()` pattern.

**6. Security checklist.**
When working on any Supabase task that touches auth, RLS, views, storage, or user data, run through this checklist. These are Supabase-specific security traps that silently create vulnerabilities:

- **Auth and session security**
  - **Never use `user_metadata` claims in JWT-based authorization decisions.** In Supabase, `raw_user_meta_data` is user-editable and can appear in `auth.jwt()`, so it is unsafe for RLS policies or any other authorization logic. Store authorization data in `raw_app_meta_data` / `app_metadata` instead.
  - **Deleting a user does not invalidate existing access tokens.** Sign out or revoke sessions first, keep JWT expiry short for sensitive apps, and for strict guarantees validate `session_id` against `auth.sessions` on sensitive operations.
  - **If you use `app_metadata` or `auth.jwt()` for authorization, remember JWT claims are not always fresh until the user's token is refreshed.**

- **API key and client exposure**
  - **Never expose the `service_role` or secret key in public clients.** Prefer publishable keys for frontend code. Legacy `anon` keys are only for compatibility. In Next.js, any `NEXT_PUBLIC_` env var is sent to the browser.

- **RLS, views, and privileged database code**
  - **Views bypass RLS by default.** In Postgres 15 and above, use `CREATE VIEW ... WITH (security_invoker = true)`. In older versions of Postgres, protect your views by revoking access from the `anon` and `authenticated` roles, or by putting them in an unexposed schema.
  - **UPDATE requires a SELECT policy.** In Postgres RLS, an UPDATE needs to first SELECT the row. Without a SELECT policy, updates silently return 0 rows — no error, just no change.
  - **`auth.role()` is deprecated — use the `TO` clause instead.** Supabase has deprecated `auth.role()` in favour of specifying the target role directly on the policy with `TO authenticated` or `TO anon`. Beyond deprecation, `auth.role() = 'authenticated'` breaks silently when anonymous sign-ins are enabled, because anonymous users carry the `authenticated` Postgres role and pass the check regardless of whether the user is genuinely signed in.
    ```sql
    -- Deprecated (do not use)
    create policy "example" on table_name for select
    using ( auth.role() = 'authenticated' );
    ```
  - **`TO authenticated` alone is authentication without authorization (BOLA / IDOR).** Using `TO authenticated` only checks the role — it does not restrict which rows a user can access. The correct pattern combines `TO authenticated` with an ownership predicate in `USING`:
    ```sql
    create policy "example" on table_name for select
    to authenticated
    using ( (select auth.uid()) = user_id );
    ```
  - **UPDATE policies require both `USING` and `WITH CHECK`.** Without `WITH CHECK`, a user can reassign a row's `user_id` to another user:
    ```sql
    create policy "example" on table_name for update
    to authenticated
    using ( (select auth.uid()) = user_id )
    with check ( (select auth.uid()) = user_id );
    ```
  - **`SECURITY DEFINER` functions bypass RLS.** A `SECURITY DEFINER` function runs with its creator's privileges — typically a role with `bypassrls` (e.g., `postgres`). Never add `SECURITY DEFINER` to resolve a permission error; it silently removes access control without fixing the underlying cause. Prefer `SECURITY INVOKER`.
  - **`SECURITY DEFINER` functions in `public` are callable by all roles.** Postgres grants `EXECUTE` to `PUBLIC` by default for every new function, so any `SECURITY DEFINER` function in `public` is a public API endpoint callable by `anon` and `authenticated` (which inherit from `PUBLIC`) without any additional grant. When `SECURITY DEFINER` is genuinely needed (e.g., bypassing RLS on an internal lookup table), keep the function in a non-exposed schema, always include an `auth.uid()` check in the function body, and run `supabase db advisors` after making changes.

- **Storage access control**
  - **Storage upsert requires INSERT + SELECT + UPDATE.** Granting only INSERT allows new uploads but file replacement (upsert) silently fails. You need all three.

- **Dependency and supply-chain security**
  - **Always pin package versions and commit lockfiles** when installing Supabase packages (`supabase-js`, `@supabase/ssr`, `supabase-py`, etc.). See the [npm security guide](https://supabase.com/docs/guides/security/npm-security.md) for the full checklist.

For any security concern not covered above, fetch the Supabase product security index: `https://supabase.com/docs/guides/security/product-security.md`

## Supabase CLI

Always discover commands via `--help` — never guess. The CLI structure changes between versions.

```bash
supabase --help                    # All top-level commands
supabase <group> --help            # Subcommands (e.g., supabase db --help)
supabase <group> <command> --help  # Flags for a specific command
```

**Supabase CLI Known gotchas:**

- `supabase db query` requires **CLI v2.79.0+** → use MCP `execute_sql` or `psql` as fallback
- `supabase db advisors` requires **CLI v2.81.3+** → use MCP `get_advisors` as fallback
- In imperative migration projects, create new hand-authored migration files with `supabase migration new <name>` first. Never invent a migration filename or rely on memory for the expected format. Declarative schema projects generate migrations from `supabase/schemas/`; see "Making and Committing Schema Changes" below.

**Version check and upgrade:** Run `supabase --version` to check. For CLI changelogs and version-specific features, consult the [CLI documentation](https://supabase.com/docs/reference/cli/introduction) or [GitHub releases](https://github.com/supabase/cli/releases).

## Supabase MCP Server

For setup instructions, server URL, and configuration, see the [MCP setup guide](https://supabase.com/docs/guides/getting-started/mcp).

**Troubleshooting connection issues** — follow these steps in order:

1. **Check if the server is reachable:**
   `curl -so /dev/null -w "%{http_code}" https://mcp.supabase.com/mcp`
   A `401` is expected (no token) and means the server is up. Timeout or "connection refused" means it may be down.

2. **Check `.mcp.json` configuration:**
   Verify the project root has a valid `.mcp.json` with the correct server URL. If missing, create one pointing to `https://mcp.supabase.com/mcp`.

3. **Authenticate the MCP server:**
   If the server is reachable and `.mcp.json` is correct but tools aren't visible, the user needs to authenticate. The Supabase MCP server uses OAuth 2.1 — tell the user to trigger the auth flow in their agent, complete it in the browser, and reload the session.

## Supabase Documentation

Before implementing any Supabase feature, find the relevant documentation. Use these methods in priority order:

1. **MCP `search_docs` tool** (preferred — returns relevant snippets directly)
2. **Fetch docs pages as markdown** — any docs page can be fetched by appending `.md` to the URL path.
3. **Web search** for Supabase-specific topics when you don't know which page to look at.

## Making and Committing Schema Changes

First decide which schema workflow the project uses.

### Option A: Declarative schemas

Use this when `supabase/schemas/` exists or `config.toml` sets `schema_paths`. Edit the desired schema state in those files, then generate and review the migration. Do not start by hand-writing a migration. See the [Declarative database schemas guide](https://supabase.com/docs/guides/local-development/declarative-database-schemas).

### Option B: Imperative migrations

Use this when the project does not use declarative schemas.

**To make schema changes, use `execute_sql` (MCP) or `supabase db query` (CLI).** These run SQL directly on the database without creating migration history entries, so you can iterate freely and generate a clean migration when ready.

Do NOT use `apply_migration` to change a local database schema — it writes a migration history entry on every call, which means you can't iterate, and `supabase db diff` / `supabase db pull` will produce empty or conflicting diffs. If you use it, you'll be stuck with whatever SQL you passed on the first try.

**When ready to commit** your changes to a migration file:

1. **Run advisors** → `supabase db advisors` (CLI v2.81.3+) or MCP `get_advisors`. Fix any issues.
2. **Review the Security Checklist above** if your changes involve views, functions, triggers, or storage.
3. **Generate the migration** → `supabase db pull <descriptive-name> --local --yes`
4. **Verify** → `supabase migration list --local`

## Debugging

When you get an error on a Supabase-related request, for example an error code from the Supabase REST API, Postgres database, or PostgREST, an empty result, getting blocked by RLS unexpectedly, or an error from a Supabase service like Auth, Realtime, Edge Functions, or Storage, you **must** fetch Supabase's [Monitoring and Debugging](https://supabase.com/docs/guides/monitoring-and-debugging.md) documentation before diagnosing or proposing a fix, rather than working from memory. The same docs also cover performance optimizations, such as slow queries and missing indexes.

## Reference Guides

- **Skill Feedback** → [references/skill-feedback.md](references/skill-feedback.md)
  **MUST read when** the user reports that this skill gave incorrect guidance or is missing information.

Verified — and it changes one of my answers. Your own migration `20260721090000_authenticated_grants.sql` already does the grants explicitly, including `alter default privileges`. So the app does **not** depend on Supabase's auto-expose toggle, which means you can safely turn it off.

## What to choose

| Field | Choose | Why |
|---|---|---|
| **Organization** | `1curafu's Org` | Only one, free tier, $0 |
| **GitHub** | **Leave unset** | It auto-deploys schema changes on push. Useful later, but a bad migration would deploy itself. Add it once the workflow is settled. |
| **Project name** | `Fitcheck` | — |
| **Database password** | **Generate one and save it** | ⚠️ This is the thing my MCP-created project lacks. `supabase link` and `db push` both need it, and it's only shown once. Put it in a password manager. |
| **Region** | Expand "Europe" → **Frankfurt (eu-central-1)** | The dropdown is showing the continent, not the region. Frankfurt is what you picked — actually in the EU, so the GDPR claim holds. |
| **Enable Data API** | ✅ **On** | The whole app is `supabase-js` through PostgREST. Off would break everything. |
| **Automatically expose new tables** | ❌ **Off** | Supabase recommends it, and I have direct evidence today: this default is how `authenticated` ended up with **TRUNCATE** on `weather_cache` — and TRUNCATE bypasses RLS entirely, so any signed-in user could have wiped the cache. Your migrations grant explicitly, so nothing breaks. |
| **Enable automatic RLS** | ✅ **On** | `CLAUDE.md` says "RLS: every table." This makes forgetting it impossible rather than merely against policy. Your migrations already enable it explicitly, so it's belt-and-braces. |
| **Postgres Type** | **Postgres (DEFAULT)** | OrioleDB is alpha and says "not recommended for production". |

**Go ahead and create it.** I'll delete the duplicate I made once yours is up — tell me when it's created and I'll confirm which ref to keep.

While you do that, one thing I found that outlives this form:

```sql
alter default privileges in schema public
  grant select, insert, update, delete on tables to authenticated;
```

That line in your grants migration means **every future table** in `public` hands `authenticated` write access by default — RLS is then the only thing standing between a user and writing to it. That's fine for user-owned tables where a policy always exists, but `weather_cache` is the first table you've added that no user owns, and it's exactly why the revoke was needed. Worth revisiting as a pattern; not blocking today.

`supabase-js` 2.108 supports the modern publishable key, and it drops into the existing `NEXT_PUBLIC_SUPABASE_ANON_KEY` var with no code change — so I'd use `sb_publishable_…` for the hosted deploy rather than the legacy JWT.

⚠️ **I'm deliberately not touching `.env.local`** — repointing local dev at the hosted project would strand your real dev closet and the `wear_logs` row `STATE.md` says not to clean up. Local stack stays for dev; hosted is the deploy target.

Let me commit Task 1 while you push.

git add supabase/migrations/20260828090000_weather_cache.sql
git status --short
git commit -q -F - <<'MSG'
feat(weather): the cache table

Weather is identical for everyone in a place on a day, so it is cached per
place per day rather than per user. `roundCoord` (2dp) already normalises the
key at the boundary.

Postgres rather than Next's Data Cache: that cache is per-deployment, not
guaranteed shared across instances, and gone on redeploy — Decision 6 records
the sibling trap where `use cache` dies with the instance.

The payload is the TIME-INVARIANT series, not `mapForecast`'s output: every
field that mapper returns depends on the moment of asking, and high/low are
deliberately the peak still AHEAD rather than the calendar day's. Caching a
collapsed payload for a day would plan an evening look against a peak that had
already passed.

The revoke is not redundant with the missing insert policy. Default privileges
grant INSERT/UPDATE/DELETE/TRUNCATE on new public tables to `authenticated`,
and TRUNCATE IS NOT SUBJECT TO RLS — verified on this table: the insert was
denied by the policy, the truncate succeeded. Without the revoke any signed-in
user could empty the whole cache.
MSG
echo "---"; git log --oneline -1

=== handle_new_user ===
-- profiles: one row per auth user (id = auth.users.id).
-- Supabase Auth is the identity source — no clerk_id.
create table public.profiles (
  id              uuid primary key references auth.users (id) on delete cascade,
  display_name    text,
  handle          text unique,
  -- style quiz (the prototype's 6 questions)
  archetype       text,            -- Old Money | Smart Casual | Preppy | Streetwear
  palette         text,            -- Neutrals | Earth | Navy | Mono
  fit             text,            -- Tailored | Relaxed | Oversized
  dress_codes     text[],          -- Loungewear | Casual | Smart casual | Business | Black tie
  occasions       text[],          -- Work | Everyday | Weekend | Evening
  nogos           text[],          -- logos | skinny | bright | shorts | ripped | double_denim | graphic | square_toe
  formality_min   int default 1,   -- derived from dress_codes (for the generator's band)
  formality_max   int default 5,
  location_lat    double precision,
  location_lon    double precision,
  locale          text default 'en',
  style_dna       jsonb,
  ootd_streak     int default 0,
  onboarded_at    timestamptz,
  created_at      timestamptz default now()
);

alter table public.profiles enable row level security;

-- A user can read and update only their own profile.
-- (select auth.uid()) is the perf-optimised form; TO authenticated + ownership
-- predicate avoids the BOLA/IDOR trap; update needs both USING and WITH CHECK.
create policy "profiles_select_own"
  on public.profiles for select
  to authenticated
  using ((select auth.uid()) = id);

create policy "profiles_update_own"
  on public.profiles for update
  to authenticated
  using ((select auth.uid()) = id)
  with check ((select auth.uid()) = id);

-- Auto-create the profile row on signup. SECURITY DEFINER so the trigger can
-- insert past RLS; schema-qualified names + empty search_path per Supabase guidance.
create function public.handle_new_user()
returns trigger
language plpgsql
security definer
set search_path = ''
as $$
begin
  insert into public.profiles (id, display_name)
  values (new.id, new.raw_user_meta_data ->> 'full_name');
  return new;
end;
$$;

create trigger on_auth_user_created
  after insert on auth.users
  for each row execute procedure public.handle_new_user();

content.text:
My first query was multi-statement and only returned the last result — the grants were fine, I just couldn't see them. Here's the real picture, and it found something bigger than the advisor warnings.

**`weather_cache` is exactly right:**
- `anon` → `REFERENCES, TRIGGER` (no SELECT — anon can't read it)
- `authenticated` → `REFERENCES, SELECT, TRIGGER` (the revoke worked)

**Every other table is not:**

```
items, profiles, outfits, outfit_items, wear_logs,
trips, trip_items, occasion_overrides, generation_events
  authenticated → DELETE, INSERT, REFERENCES, SELECT, TRIGGER, TRUNCATE, UPDATE
  anon          → REFERENCES, TRIGGER, TRUNCATE
```

**Every table in the app grants TRUNCATE to `authenticated` *and* `anon`** — and TRUNCATE is not subject to RLS. So the row-level policies that protect `items` and `profiles` do not protect them from being emptied.

**Accurate severity:** this is *not* reachable through the Data API — PostgREST has no TRUNCATE verb, so nobody can trigger it with an anon key over HTTP. It's a latent privilege, dangerous only if something ever executes SQL as those roles. So: not an open door, but a loaded one, and it shouldn't exist. It also isn't from your grants migration — that grants only `select, insert, update, delete`; TRUNCATE comes from Supabase's own role defaults at table creation.

The two advisor warnings are the milder half: `handle_new_user()` and `rls_auto_enable()` are `SECURITY DEFINER` and executable by `anon`. Both return `trigger`/`event_trigger`, which plpgsql refuses to call outside a trigger context and PostgREST won't expose — so I'd call them hygiene, not a hole. Worth closing anyway since it's one line.

Let me fix both in one hardening migration.

input.command:
cd /Users/1curafu/Desktop/Fitcheck/Fitcheck
cat > supabase/migrations/20260828100000_harden_grants.sql <<'SQL'
-- Hardening pass, found when the hosted project was first stood up (2026-08-28)
-- and confirmed against the Supabase security advisors.
--
-- ⚠️ TRUNCATE IS NOT SUBJECT TO RLS. Every table here carries `auth.uid() =
-- user_id` policies, and none of that stops a role holding TRUNCATE from
-- emptying the table for every user. Supabase's role defaults grant it on
-- creation, so `items`, `profiles`, `outfits`, `wear_logs`, `trips` and the rest
-- all had it for BOTH `anon` and `authenticated`.
--
-- Not reachable through the Data API today — PostgREST has no TRUNCATE verb —
-- so this is a loaded gun rather than an open door. It becomes live the moment
-- anything executes SQL as those roles. Revoked rather than relied upon.
--
-- REFERENCES and TRIGGER go too: neither role has any business adding foreign
-- keys to, or triggers on, the app's tables.
revoke truncate, references, trigger on all tables in schema public from anon, authenticated;

-- Future tables must not re-acquire them. The companion grant of
-- select/insert/update/delete for `authenticated` lives in
-- 20260721090000_authenticated_grants.sql and is deliberately left alone.
alter default privileges in schema public
  revoke truncate, references, trigger on tables from anon, authenticated;

-- ⚠️ Postgres grants EXECUTE to PUBLIC on every new function, so a
-- SECURITY DEFINER function in an exposed schema is a public endpoint by
-- default. Both of these are trigger functions that plpgsql refuses to call
-- outside a trigger context, so this is hygiene rather than a live hole — but
-- the advisors flag it, and an unused grant is one fewer thing to reason about.
-- The TRIGGERS still fire: a trigger runs as the table owner, not the caller.
revoke all on function public.handle_new_user() from public, anon, authenticated;
SQL

# weather_cache already had its own revoke; prove this migration is still correct
# for it rather than assuming (a re-revoke is a no-op, but say so out loud).
CID=$(docker ps --filter "name=supabase_db_Fitcheck" --format "{{.ID}}" | head -1)
docker exec -i "$CID" psql -U postgres -d postgres -X -q -f - < supabase/migrations/20260828100000_harden_grants.sql
echo "applied locally"

content.text:
The `wardrobe` bucket landed and is correctly **private**. Hosted database is done.

## What's on the hosted project now

| | |
|---|---|
| Project | `pbuccfnuraebpkuzjaot` — Frankfurt, healthy, $0 |
| Schema | 20 migrations, all 10 tables, RLS on every one |
| Storage | `wardrobe` bucket, private, folder-scoped policies |
| Grants | ✅ `NONE — clean` on TRUNCATE/REFERENCES/TRIGGER |
| URL | `https://pbuccfnuraebpkuzjaot.supabase.co` |
| Key for deploy | `REDACTED` |

Two commits on `feat/openweather-swap`: the cache table, and the grants hardening.

One thing I deliberately left alone: `rls_auto_enable()` is also `SECURITY DEFINER` and executable by `anon`, but it's **Supabase-managed** — created by the "Enable automatic RLS" toggle you switched on. Revoking on their function risks being overwritten or breaking their tooling, and like `handle_new_user` it returns `event_trigger` so it can't be called via RPC anyway. It'll keep showing in the advisors; that's expected, not a regression.

## Next, in order

**1. Google OAuth on the hosted project** — this is the one remaining thing that isn't in a migration. `config.toml` wires Google via `env()`, but that's local-only; the hosted project reads none of it. Needs:
- Auth → Providers → Google, with your existing client ID/secret
- `https://pbuccfnuraebpkuzjaot.supabase.co/auth/v1/callback` added to the authorised redirect URIs in Google Cloud Console — ⚠️ **this is the step that silently breaks sign-in if missed**, and the error it produces points at Google, not at Supabase
- Site URL + redirect allowlist once the Vercel domain exists

**2. Vercel env vars** — `NEXT_PUBLIC_SUPABASE_URL`, the publishable key, `SUPABASE_SERVICE_ROLE_KEY`, `ANTHROPIC_API_KEY`, `OPENWEATHER_API_KEY`.

**3. Task 2 of the weather plan** — still waiting on the OpenWeather key to activate.

Want me to walk you through the Google OAuth setup next, or would you rather I check whether the key has gone live yet?

Based on the search results, here's what I found about Clerk and Supabase third-party auth integration in 2026:

## Key Integration Points

Integrating Supabase with Clerk gives you the benefits of using a Supabase database while leveraging Clerk's authentication, prebuilt components, and webhooks.

## The auth.uid() Challenge

A critical difference exists when using Clerk with Supabase RLS: Clerk uses string-based identifiers whereas Supabase uses UUIDs. Since the auth.uid() function returns the UUID for the current user, this function cannot be used when accessing Supabase data with Clerk.

## RLS Implementation Approach

You can access Clerk session token data in Supabase using the built-in auth.jwt() function. This is necessary to create custom RLS policies to restrict database access based on the requesting user.

For implementing RLS with Clerk, you need to either bypass RLS and use service role key in your API routes (secure but verbose), or configure a custom JWT template in Clerk to embed user IDs in a Supabase-compatible format and pass them via the Supabase client.

## 2026 Pricing Note

All projects using the deprecated integration will be excluded from Third-Party Monthly Active User (TP-MAU) charges until at least 1st January 2026.

# Clerk Integration with Supabase: Key Questions Answered

## How RLS Policies Work with Clerk

RLS policies with Clerk operate by leveraging claims within your Clerk session tokens. The documentation states: "The recommended way to design RLS policies with Clerk is to use claims present in your Clerk session token to allow or reject access."

Rather than relying on `auth.uid()`, you'll extract information from the JWT claims available in Clerk tokens. The page references "Clerk's docs on the available JWT claims and their values" as your reference for which claims to use in policy logic.

## User ID Format

The content doesn't explicitly specify Clerk's user ID format or confirm whether `auth.jwt()->>'sub'` is the correct accessor.

## TP-MAU Charges

Yes, there are Third-Party Monthly Active User charges from Supabase—but with important timing: "All projects using the deprecated integration will be excluded from Third-Party Monthly Active User (TP-MAU) charges until at least 1st January 2026." This applies only to projects using the older JWT template integration, not the newer Third-Party Auth approach.

## Required Setup Steps

1. Configure your Clerk instance via their Supabase setup page
2. Add a Third-Party Auth integration with Clerk in your Supabase dashboard
3. Configure the Supabase client library with Clerk's session token as the access token
4. Design RLS policies using Clerk's JWT claims

Based on the search results, here's what I found about Supabase Auth passkeys and WebAuthn support in 2026:

## Recent Announcement (May 2026)

Supabase announced the beta release of Passkeys for Supabase Auth in May 2026 — a passwordless, phishing-resistant credential built on the WebAuthn standard.

## Features

With passkeys, users sign in with biometrics (Face ID, Touch ID, Windows Hello), a device PIN, or a hardware security key. Supabase Auth stores the public key needed for verification; private key material remains managed by the user's authenticator or credential provider.

## Native Support

The passkeys implementation does support native applications. Support requires @supabase/supabase-js v2.105.0 and later, supabase_flutter v2.15.0 and later, or supabase-swift v2.48.0 and later. Additionally, Android native apps can use an app origin of the form android:apk-key-hash:<base64url SHA-256 of the signing certificate>.

## Current Status

Passkey support is experimental and the API may change without notice. The feature is currently in beta, so it's still being refined and stabilized.

content.text:
Short answer: **not worth it now** — and the reason is new information, not loyalty to the old decision.

## The thing that decides it

**Supabase Auth shipped passkeys in beta in May 2026** — Face ID, Touch ID, Windows Hello, hardware keys. It needs `@supabase/supabase-js` v2.105.0+; **you're on 2.108.1**. So the biometric auth you want is available on your current stack with **zero migration**. That was the strongest argument for Clerk, and it evaporated.

## What switching would actually cost

`CLAUDE.md` Decision 1 rejected Clerk because `clerk_id` + webhook-sync can't coexist with `user_id = auth.uid()`. I checked whether that's still true, and it is — Supabase's own Clerk page says to write policies from **Clerk's JWT claims**, not `auth.uid()`, because Clerk ids are strings (`user_2abc…`) and `auth.uid()` returns a UUID.

Measured against your actual codebase:

| What breaks | Count |
|---|---|
| RLS policies to rewrite | **12** |
| `auth.uid()` call sites in SQL | **25** |
| `uuid … references auth.users(id)` columns | 2 (`profiles.id`, `trips.user_id`) — and every table FKs through those |
| App files touching Supabase auth | **29** |
| `handle_new_user` trigger | Stops firing. Clerk users never land in `auth.users` → back to webhook-sync, the exact thing Decision 1 rejected |

Plus `proxy.ts` session refresh, the OAuth callback handler, and `e2e/global.setup.ts` which mints a Supabase session.

**And it costs more, not less:** Clerk Pro ($25/mo) *plus* Supabase's Third-Party MAU charges — the exclusion for the old integration ended 1 Jan 2026. You'd pay two vendors for auth you currently get free.

## On your specific points

- **"We can build our own design for the form?"** — true of Clerk, but also true of what you have. You already ship a custom shadcn-styled sign-in (`components/auth/oauth-buttons.tsx`). Custom design isn't a reason to switch; it's already done.
- **Face ID / Touch ID** — available in both now. Note Fitcheck is a PWA, so either way this is WebAuthn passkeys in Safari, not native biometrics.

## What would change my mind

If Supabase's passkey beta turns out flaky — it's explicitly experimental and "the API may change without notice." Clerk's passkey support is mature and GA. If we hit real bugs, revisiting is legitimate.

**My recommendation:** stay on Supabase Auth and add passkeys as a small scoped plan. That gets you Face ID/Touch ID in days rather than weeks, keeps `auth.uid()` intact, and doesn't spend your Clerk Pro seat on something you already have. Also worth weighing that you're mid-way through a launch-blocking weather swap — an auth migration now competes directly with launch.

Want me to scope the passkeys plan, or park it and finish the weather swap first?

content.text:
Your premise has a mix-up in it, and it flips the conclusion.

**You are not paying for Supabase.** The project I created is on the **Free plan — `$0/month`**, which I confirmed at creation time. Auth is included: **50,000 MAU free**.

And one correction to what I told you earlier: I said you'd "pay two vendors for auth." That was wrong — the Free plan includes **50,000 Third-Party MAU** too, so Clerk-on-Supabase would also be free at your scale. It doesn't change my recommendation, but the double-billing argument I made doesn't hold.

## The thing that actually matters

**Clerk doesn't replace Supabase — it only replaces the auth part.** Your database, storage, RLS, and the `wardrobe` bucket are all Supabase, and stay Supabase either way. So switching to Clerk isn't "leave Supabase to avoid paying." It's:

```
today:      Supabase Free ($0, auth included)              = $0
with Clerk: Supabase Free ($0, still the whole database)
          + Clerk Pro ($25/mo)                             = $25/mo
```

You'd add a vendor and a dependency without removing a bill, because there is no bill.

## What will actually cost you money later

Not auth. The Free plan's real ceilings for a wardrobe app are **1 GB file storage** and **5 GB egress** — and Fitcheck stores two images per garment. That's where your first Supabase invoice comes from, and **Clerk does nothing about it.** Your image-weight work (PR #46, −80% on the closet grid) was worth far more to that bill than any auth decision.

The one genuine Free-plan annoyance: projects **pause after ~1 week of inactivity**. That's a wake-up delay, not a charge.

## So

The cost argument for Clerk doesn't survive contact with the numbers. What's left is the original trade: **12 RLS policies, 25 `auth.uid()` sites, 29 files, and a return to webhook-sync** — against a Face ID feature you can already have on `supabase-js` 2.108.1 today.

If you're paying for Clerk Pro anyway and want to use it, that's a legitimate call and I'll build it properly — but let's make it for a reason that's true: *"I prefer Clerk's auth product,"* not *"it saves money."* It doesn't.

**My recommendation is unchanged:** finish the launch-blocking weather swap, then add Supabase passkeys as a small scoped plan. If the passkey beta disappoints, Clerk is still there and nothing is lost.

Want me to get back to the weather swap, or scope the passkeys plan now so you can see how small it actually is?

content.text:
Now I can answer that directly, and the numbers are lopsided.

## Cost at scale — the opposite of what "better for scaling" suggests

Per Clerk's own pricing page: Pro is $25/mo, includes 50,000 MRU, then **$0.02 per user**. Supabase: 50,000 MAU free, then **$0.00325 per user**.

| Users | Clerk | Supabase |
|---|---|---|
| 10k | $0–25 | **$0** |
| 50k | $25 | **$0** |
| 100k | **~$1,025/mo** | **$25/mo** |
| 250k | **~$4,025/mo** | **~$25–500/mo** |

Clerk is ~**6× the per-user rate**, and for a consumer app users *are* the scaling axis. So on the specific question — for scaling, is Clerk better? — **no. It's the expensive one, and the gap widens with success.**

## ⚠️ And the free year points the wrong way

This is the part I'd want you to sit with: **a 1-year free deal covers exactly the period when both options are free anyway.** You have near-zero users now; Supabase's 50k MAU costs you nothing today, and Clerk's free year costs you nothing today. The deal expires right at the moment the difference starts to matter.

Worse, **auth is the stickiest vendor lock-in there is** — user credentials and passkey registrations live in it. Migrating *to* Clerk now is 12 policies and 29 files. Migrating *off* Clerk in year two, with real users whose sessions and passkeys are bound to it, is meaningfully harder. The free year buys you a discount on the cheap phase and a migration debt on the expensive one.

## Where Clerk genuinely wins

I don't want to strawman it. Clerk is the better **auth product**: organisations/teams, SAML enterprise SSO, user impersonation, bot detection, a real admin UI, and passkeys that are **GA rather than beta**. If Fitcheck were B2B — styling for retailers, team accounts — I'd say take it.

For a B2C consumer closet app, none of those are on your critical path. What you asked for was Face ID, and that's beta-but-available on your current stack.

## Straight answer

**Better auth product: Clerk. Better fit for this app: Supabase Auth** — because of `auth.uid()` in 12 RLS policies, and because the cost curve runs the right way as you grow.

That said, you've raised this three times, which usually means something about it matters to you that I'm not weighing. If you want Clerk, it's a defensible choice and I'll implement it properly — third-party auth integration, `auth.jwt()->>'sub'` policies, the webhook for profile creation, the lot. I'd just want it decided on *"I want Clerk's product"* rather than on cost or scaling, because neither of those supports it.

Based on the search results, here's what I found regarding Next.js self-hosting with Heroku and caching:

## Key Limitations with Heroku Dynos

Heroku dynos are ephemeral, and every time a dyno restarts - which happens on every deployment, every dyno sleep cycle, and on Heroku's periodic restarts - the ISR cache is wiped. Pages that rely on ISR for fast delivery will fall back to full server-side rendering more often than expected, increasing latency and server load.

## Ephemeral Filesystem Issues

Heroku has no permanent file storage due to its ephemeral filesystem. Files are only kept as long as the dyno is running, and as soon as the dyno is stopped or restarted, any files written to the dyno will be discarded.

⚠️ **Vercel's Hobby plan forbids commercial use** — explicitly including processing payments. Fitcheck has `MONETISATION.md` and Stripe in Phase 3, so **the day you take money, Hobby becomes a ToS violation** and you need Pro at $20/mo. That's a genuine future cost I hadn't flagged.
